pos: n. & adj. (a refutation of error; polemics, the branch of theology that defends the truth against it)
etymology: Greek polemikos, warlike, from polemos, war, through French polémique. Webster (1828) enters POLEM’IC, POLEM’ICAL, “[Gr. war.]”
biblical_def: A polemic is an argument made against an error in defense of the truth. Webster (1828) defines the adjective as “controversial; disputative; intended to maintain an opinion or system in opposition to others,” and the noun as “a disputant; a controvertist.” Polemics is the branch of theology that does this work on purpose: it names false doctrine, shows from Scripture where it fails, and calls the erring back. Apologetics answers the unbeliever who asks “a reason of the hope” (1Pe 3:15); polemics answers the false teacher inside the camp. Scripture commands it. Jude wrote to exhort the church to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). An elder must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). Apollos “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28), and Paul withstood Peter “to the face, because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11). The same Scripture governs the manner: “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). The weapon is the Word, not the fist: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): POLEMIC, POLEMICAL, controversial; disputative; intended to maintain an opinion or system in opposition to others. As a noun, a disputant; a controvertist.
webster_full: 1. Controversial; disputative; intended to maintain an opinion or system in opposition to others; as a polemic treatise, discourse, essay or book; polemic divinity.
2. Engaged in supporting an opinion or system by controversy; as a polemic writer.
POLEM'IC, noun A disputant; a controvertist; one who writes in support of an opinion or system in opposition to another.
scriptures: Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.

corruption_summary: Modern speech uses polemical to mean merely harsh or mean-spirited, and much of the modern church treats any public refutation of error as a failure of love. The opposite abuse turns polemics into a blood sport.
corruption_paragraphs: In common use polemical has come to mean angry, one-sided or unfair, and a sermon that names a false teacher is dismissed as “too polemical” before its argument is weighed. Behind the label is a new rule that love never contradicts. Scripture knows no such rule. The Lord Jesus told the Sadducees to their faces, “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God” (Mat 22:29). A church that will not refute error has not become gentler; it has left its sheep to men “who subvert whole houses” (Tit 1:11).

The opposite abuse is polemics as sport. The man who contends in order to win, to gather a following, or to vent his own temper has not taken up the sword of the Spirit; he has carried the “wars and fightings” of his own lusts into the church (Jas 4:1). Biblical polemic is aimed at error that destroys souls, not at every brother who differs on a lesser point, and it is carried on “in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth” (2Ti 2:25). Its goal is the rescue of the erring, not the defeat of an opponent.
roots_summary: Greek polemos, war, through polemikos, warlike: theology that makes war on error with the Word of God.
roots_lines: Greek polemikos, of or for war; French polémique, a controversy; English polemic.
Webster (1828): controversial; disputative; intended to maintain an opinion or system in opposition to others.
Polemic divinity: the older name for theology written against error, also called elenctic theology, as in Francis Turretin’s Institutes of Elenctic Theology (1679–1685).
Earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints (Jud 1:3).
usage: polemic divinity, the theology of controversy
a polemic against the errors of Rome
the polemical writings of Athanasius against the Arians
